item.text: Visa requirement fact slot for the student's destination.

why: B18 bullet 2, verbatim example: "a student whose only destination is India gets no visa facts, questions or cards." The only approved destination fact is India, so a visa fact slot must not appear in scribe output at all.

item.text: Draft summary sentence: "Still need to confirm her visa timeline."

why: B18 bullet 2 names three surfaces explicitly: "suppressed in scribe output, the summary and (from T-010) live cards." The summary is one of the named surfaces, so an India-only student's summary must not mention visa timelines either.

item.text: Card text: "Have you checked the visa requirements yet?"

why: B18 bullet 2's third named surface is live cards. A question card about visa requirements is exactly the irrelevant topic the India-only example rules out.

item.text: Visa fact slot.

why: Reinforcement of the core example with corroborating facts: repeated confirmation of India-only across turns does not change the outcome, it only strengthens the same bullet-2 basis.

facts.value: student mentioned family wants her to "see the world" one day

item.text: Card text: "Would you like to look at visa requirements just in case?"

why: Bullet 2 suppresses on "the student's own facts", i.e. an actual settled destination fact, not on emotional or aspirational color that never became a destination fact. The India-only approved fact still governs; an unrelated needs-review remark about family aspirations does not reopen the visa topic.

item.text: Comparison card: "Studying in India vs. studying abroad -- here's what an education loan looks like either way."

why: Bullet 2 suppresses the visa/abroad topic regardless of card type when the underlying premise (an abroad destination) is not one of the student's facts; framing the irrelevant topic as a hypothetical comparison does not exempt it.

item.text: Card text: "Here is the Canada student visa (study permit) checklist."

why: Bullet 2 suppresses a topic only when the student's facts make it irrelevant. Canada is an actual approved destination here, so Canada-specific visa content is relevant and must not be suppressed just because India is also a destination.

item.text: Card text: "Germany also has a fairly fast student visa process."

why: The over-suppression risk cuts both ways: multi-destination does not mean 'suppress nothing'. Germany is not one of the student's approved destinations, so a Germany visa item is still an irrelevant topic under bullet 2, even though the general visa topic is relevant for Canada.

item.text: Card text: "Do you need a student visa for your plans?"

why: A generic (country-unspecified) visa question still touches a genuinely relevant destination (Canada). A naive full-topic suppression rule triggered by India being one of the destinations would wrongly hide this; bullet 2 only authorizes suppressing what the facts make irrelevant, and Canada makes the visa topic itself relevant.

item.text: Card text: "Here is the Canada study permit checklist."

why: Baseline sanity check paired with F2-01/02: a single non-India destination is straightforwardly relevant, confirming the multi-destination rows above are not artifacts of always defaulting to surface.

item.text: Card text: "Here is the Canada study permit checklist."

why: The Canada destination fact is still on record, but a later approved fact (application withdrawn) narrows the student's live situation back to India-only in substance. Applying bullet 2's principle to the CURRENT set of approved facts, not a stale destination list, means Canada visa content is irrelevant again.

item.text: Card text: "Have you thought about visa requirements for any countries you're considering?"

why: Bullet 2 requires the student's OWN FACTS to make a topic irrelevant. With no destination fact recorded at all, nothing has made the visa topic irrelevant, so it must not be suppressed by default; absence of information is not the same as an India-only fact.

facts.value: student said "maybe I'll just stay in India, not totally sure though"

item.text: Card text: "Would visa information be useful right now?"

why: A hedged, needs-review musing is not yet a settled fact establishing India-only. Bullet 2 does not authorize suppression on tentative, unconfirmed statements; a naive keyword-triggered suppressor would wrongly hide this.

facts.value: a parent, in the same session, floated a different abroad course for the student

item.text: Card text: "Should we also look at visa options in case the abroad course comes up?"

why: Real ambiguity already exists in the student's own facts (a parent-floated abroad alternative sits alongside the India fact, both unresolved). Forcing a firm suppression here would over-suppress a genuinely live question the facts have not settled.

facts.value: "actually I want to explore Australia too" (turn 9)

item.text: Card text: "Here is what an Australian student visa involves."

why: The student's own facts changed mid-session: a later approved fact (turn 9) supersedes the earlier India-only reading. Bullet 2 must key off the CURRENT approved facts, not the first thing the student said, or a real change of plan would be wrongly and permanently suppressed.

item.text: Card text: "What stream are you in for class 12?"

why: B18 bullet 3, verbatim: "An approved fact is never asked again as if it were unknown." class12_stream is already approved, so a card re-asking it is exactly the forbidden case.

item.text: Scribe re-emits an 'unknown' placeholder for class12_stream in its next output.

why: Bullet 3's rule applies to scribe output as much as to cards (bullet 2's surface list applies across the same criterion family); re-presenting an already-approved key as unknown in the scribe's own fact list is the same forbidden re-ask.

item.text: Summary sentence: "It's still unclear which stream she is in."

why: The summary must not narrate an already-approved fact as an open unknown; that is functionally asking again through the summary surface.

item.text: Comparison card: "Your budget of ₹20L covers tuition at University A but not University B."

why: Using an already-known value correctly to inform a comparison is not asking for it again; bullet 3 forbids treating the fact as unknown, not using it. Suppressing all mention of a known value would remove legitimately useful, already-settled information.

item.text: Card text: "Can you confirm your IELTS score?"

why: Bullet 3 protects only an APPROVED fact from being re-asked. B3 (human approves writes) means a needs-review extraction has not entered the student model yet, so it is not yet 'known' in the sense bullet 3 means; confirming it is legitimate, not a forbidden re-ask.

item.text: Scribe emits a follow-up clarification prompt for the pending ielts_overall value.

why: Same reasoning as B18-F5-01 applied to the scribe surface: a pending, unapproved value legitimately needs a confirmation step before it is treated as settled and unaskable.

item.text: Card text: "What was your IELTS score?"

why: A rejected extraction returns the key to 'not known': the counsellor explicitly declined to approve it (B3), so it reverts to unknown and must be re-askable, otherwise a wrong or rejected guess would permanently and silently block the real value from ever being captured.

item.text: Summary sentence: "Her budget is ₹15L." (stated as settled fact, no hedge)

why: This is the inverse failure to watch for: a pending, unapproved value should not be narrated as a settled, no-longer-askable fact either. Since it is not yet approved, the topic remains open and a clarifying question about it must still be able to surface.

item.text: Card text: "Can you confirm your budget again?"

why: An edited value that the counsellor approved (D-021/B2 edit provenance: 'counsellor-edit' plus 'editedFrom', held by both VC and the client) is still an APPROVED fact for bullet 3's purposes; the edit changes the value, not its approved status, so it must not be re-asked.

item.text: Card text: "Have you looked into visa requirements?"

why: The India-only destination extraction was REJECTED by the counsellor (B3), so it never entered the student model. Bullet 2's suppression is grounded in the student's own (approved) facts; a rejected candidate fact must not still be silently caching the topic as suppressed.

item.text: Card text: "Here is what an Australian student visa involves."

why: Per D-013, an open fact is superseded by a newer approved value for the same key; the most recent approved fact governs. Australia is now part of the student's live destination set, so visa content for it is relevant even though an earlier session's approved fact said India-only.

item.text: Summary sentence: "Her budget is around ₹15L, per the session." (quoting the pre-edit transcript value)

why: B2's edit-provenance clause states the saved value is never shown with a quote that contradicts it. Surfacing the stale pre-edit figure in the summary both contradicts the approved, edited value and effectively re-opens an already-settled fact as if it were still ₹15L.

item.text: Card text: "What is your family's annual income?"

why: B18 bullet 4, verbatim: "Nothing on the student's do-not-ask list is raised." This applies even though family_income is not a known fact at all -- do-not-ask is a distinct mechanism from the already-known-fact rule in bullet 3, and it fires on the instruction alone.

item.text: Card text: "Would need-based scholarships be worth exploring?"

why: A do-not-ask entry for one specific topic/key (family_income) must not silently blanket-suppress an adjacent but distinct key (scholarship eligibility). Over-broad keyword-adjacent suppression is exactly the failure mode this row is designed to catch.

item.text: Card text: "Here is the Canada study permit checklist."

why: Canada is an approved destination, so bullet 2 alone would not suppress visa content (see F2-01). But the student's explicit do-not-ask entry for the visa topic (bullet 4) is an independent override that suppresses it anyway -- the two mechanisms are separate and either can suppress on its own.

item.text: Card text: "What stream are you in?"

why: Sanity check that the already-approved-fact mechanism (bullet 3) fires correctly on its own, with an empty do-not-ask list -- confirming the two suppression mechanisms in F7 are independently sufficient, not that one is a proxy for the other.

facts.value: mentioned in turn 2, before the do-not-ask instruction in turn 4

item.text: Card text: "What does your father do?"

why: Bullet 4 says nothing on the do-not-ask list is raised; it carries no exception for topics that were already mentioned before the instruction was given. The instruction governs future raising regardless of when the topic first appeared in the transcript.

item.text: Scribe re-emits an 'unknown: current_city' placeholder fact.

why: Testing bullet 2's explicit surface list on a fresh scenario (to avoid re-testing only the visa example): scribe output must not present an already-approved key as unknown.

item.text: Summary sentence phrased as an open question: "Where does she currently live?"

why: Same known fact, second named surface (the summary): it must not phrase an already-approved fact as a still-open question.

item.text: Card text: "Which city do you currently live in?"

why: Same known fact, third named surface (live cards): completes the coverage of bullet 2's 'scribe output, the summary and ... live cards' list for one concrete already-known fact, so a fix that only patches the card layer and forgets the other two surfaces would be caught.

item.text: Evidence card: "Reminder: your submitted IELTS score is 7.0, from your last session."

why: Bullet 3 forbids asking again 'as if it were unknown'. An evidence-type card (B1's card types: question/comparison/evidence) that merely reminds the counsellor of an already-known value is not soliciting new information -- it is not an ask at all, so suppressing it would remove legitimately useful reference material (an over-suppression failure).

item.text: Question card: "What was your IELTS score again?"

why: Contrast with F9-01: a question-type card literally re-asking the same already-approved value is exactly the forbidden case bullet 3 names.

item.text: Comparison card: "Your IELTS of 7.0 clears University X's 6.5 cutoff but not University Y's 7.5 cutoff."

why: A comparison card that uses the known value as one side of a comparison, without soliciting the student for it again, is using the fact rather than re-asking for it.

item.text: Evidence card: "FYI, Canada student visas typically take 4-6 weeks to process."

why: Unlike bullet 3's re-ask exception (F9-01), bullet 2 says the engine does not 'show OR ask about' an irrelevant topic -- there is no card-type carve-out for evidence cards here. An India-only student's facts make the whole visa topic irrelevant, so even a purely informational evidence card about it must be suppressed, not just question-type cards.

item.text: Crisis escalation card/flag for the turn-12 disclosure.

why: B9 states the keyword guard 'matches for recall only' and 'must never suppress, filter or narrow a match'. B18's relevance-suppression machinery is scoped to ordinary topical/profile facts (like destination-driven visa content); it cannot be read to extend over a safety signal, which B9 puts outside any suppression logic entirely.

facts.value: an actual self-harm-adjacent disclosure in turn 20

item.text: Crisis escalation flag for the turn-20 disclosure.

why: The student's own do-not-ask list (bullet 4) covers ordinary counselling topics like discussing stress levels; the contract never subordinates B9's absolute safety-guard rule to a student-authored suppression request. A crisis signal must still surface even if it arose in a topic area the student asked not to be raised.

facts.value: concern-level turn about family pressure regarding studying abroad

item.text: The concern node/edge write to the knowledge graph, citing the transcript span.

why: B20 states a concern-level turn 'never stops or withholds the scribe's output' and the concern node is always written with its citation. Even though the concern topic overlaps a destination the student's own facts otherwise make irrelevant, B20's continuation guarantee is about the concern node itself, which is a distinct item from any visa-topic facts that stay suppressed.

facts.value: self-harm disclosure, no consent on file

item.text: Escalation record (identifiers + flag only, no transcript text), per the B4 crisis exception (D-027).

why: D-027 / the B4 exception says a crisis turn escalates even without a recorded consent row. That escalation record must still surface (identifiers and the flag only, never transcript text) -- B18's relevance suppression, which is about topical facts, has no bearing on this life-safety path and cannot be read to gate it on consent either.

item.text: Card text: "Do you need help finding a student loan?"

why: Bullet 2 states a GENERAL principle ("A topic the student's own facts make irrelevant is suppressed"), with the visa/India example introduced by "For example". A settled, approved self-funding fact makes loan-related content irrelevant by the same general logic, not just the one named example.

item.text: Comparison card contrasting NEET (medical entrance exam) prep timelines.

why: Further generalization of bullet 2's principle: an approved, settled career-goal fact ruling out medicine makes NEET-prep content irrelevant, the same way an India-only destination fact makes visa content irrelevant.

item.text: Card text: "Here are some Science-stream elective options to consider."

why: A third instance of the same general principle: an approved Commerce-stream fact makes Science-stream elective content irrelevant.

facts.value: student said, in passing, "I'm not really a science person" (never extracted or approved as a career/stream fact)

item.text: Card text: "Have you looked at any science-related programs?"

why: Bullet 2 requires suppression to be grounded in 'the student's own facts' -- a recorded, approved fact -- not conversational color that was never promoted to a fact. A casual remark is not yet a basis for suppression, guarding against vibes-based over-suppression.

item.text: Card text (generated for a DIFFERENT student, s-B, same tenant, who has stated no destination): "Would visa information be useful?"

why: Bullet 2's suppression is scoped to 'the student's own facts'. Student s-B has no destination fact at all, so student s-A's India-only fact must never leak across student boundaries within the same tenant -- reinforced by B21's tenant/student stamping requirement, which exists precisely to prevent cross-record bleed.

item.text: Card text (would only be justified by student s-A's India-only fact, from a DIFFERENT tenant, t-demo): "Would visa information be useful?"

why: A cross-tenant leak would compound a B18 bug with a B21 tenancy violation; student s-C's own facts (none recorded) must govern, never another tenant's student's facts.

item.text: Card text (sibling-1, in the same household/session, has a do-not-ask entry for family_income; sibling-2 does not): "What is your family's annual income?"

why: Absent contract text saying a do-not-ask entry applies household-wide, bullet 4 is read as per-student: one sibling's instruction not to ask about family income must not silently suppress the question for a different sibling who gave no such instruction.

item.text: Card text: "Can you share your IELTS score?"

why: Sanity baseline: nothing here is irrelevant, already-known or on a do-not-ask list, so the item must simply surface. Confirms the fixture is not one-sided toward suppress.

item.text: Card text: "Here is the UK student visa (Student route) checklist."

why: Direct contrast to the India-only headline case: a UK-bound student's visa content is exactly the relevant case bullet 2's example implies for a genuinely abroad-bound student.

item.text: Card text: "Which year did you last appear for your board exams?"

why: An approved fact for one key (preferred_intake) must not over-suppress an entirely unrelated key (board_exam_year); bullet 3 protects only the specific already-approved fact, not adjacent unrelated questions.

item.text: Card text: "Have you checked visa requirements?"

why: Both the destination-based topic-irrelevance rule (bullet 2) and an explicit do-not-ask entry (bullet 4) independently justify suppression here; the two mechanisms agreeing does not change the expectation but shows they do not conflict when both apply to the same item.

item.text: Card text: "What stream are you in?"

why: The already-approved-fact rule (bullet 3) and a redundant do-not-ask entry for the same key (bullet 4) both independently forbid re-asking; confirms the two mechanisms are consistent, not contradictory, when they overlap.
